The Data: Drought By State

Monthly, 1895-2022, lower 48 states: 48 x 1,528 months = 73,344 rows
Values: percent of state area in each class
NOAA 9-month Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), via drought.gov and TidyTuesday 2022-06-14









Columns
Meaning

the same five classes on the wet side


x0, x9
were 0 and -9 in the raw file; clean_names() renamed them

Tidy Means

Each variable is a column
Each observation is a row
Each value is a cell


d0, d1, d2, d3, d4 are five values of one variable, dryness class, spread across five columns.

What percent of Nebraska was in severe drought (d2)?

title: Module 06: Tidy Data + Your Project Repository
text:
381.3% Of Nebraska?

The classes are cumulative: each means “at least this dry”.

d2 = severe drought or worse: 79.5% of the state
Only severe, nothing worse: d2 - d3 = 79.5 - 65.7 = 13.8%
True in all 73,344 rows: d0 >= d1 >= d2 >= d3 >= d4



The code adds them without complaint. The definition catches it. Same trap as Module 05: totals stacked on the rows they total.

Recap: Module 03

What did clean_names() turn "Age (Years)" into?
filter(!is.na(x)) vs drop_na(x): same result?

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
text:
Learning Goals
By the end of today you can:

read the import message and problems(), and declare missing codes with na =
check types (glimpse, class, summary, count) and say why a number is text
fix types (parse_number, as.numeric, as.integer, col_types)
select(), filter(), arrange(), and report row counts before and after
create variables with mutate() and keep them by reassigning
render a first Quarto document

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
section: The Data: Great Lakes Fish Stocking
text:
The Data: Great Lakes Fish Stocking

Great Lakes Fishery Commission stocking database
56,232 stocking events x 31 columns, 1950-2018
Used exactly as released: real codes, real typos, real gaps
Via TidyTuesday (2021-06-08)


Ask: who has worked with agency data before? What went wrong the first time you opened it?

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
text:
Vocabulary








Term
Meaning




column type
<dbl> number, <int> integer, <chr> text, <date>, <lgl>


missing-value code
"N/A", -999, 999.99: someone’s way of saying “unknown”


coercion
converting a type; misfits become NA with a warning


parsing problem
a value read_csv() could not fit; see problems()


row count check
nrow() before and after a filter

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
text:
Cycle 1: Trustworthy Columns
stocked_raw <- read_csv(here("class", "data", "stocked.csv"))
problems(stocked_raw)          # 22 values R could not read

stocked <- read_csv(
  here("class", "data", "stocked.csv"),
  na = c("", "NA", "N/A")      # tell R what "missing" looks like
) |>
  clean_names()

glimpse(stocked)               # which <chr> columns should be numbers?
summary(stocked$length)        # 999.99? 0 mm? 13 m?

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
section: One Code Makes A Whole Column Text
text:
One Code Makes A Whole Column Text

mark_eff holds percentages, but one value is "N/A"
R cannot store "N/A" as a number, so the whole column becomes <chr>
Fix at import (na =) or after (as.numeric() + read the warning)


The dangerous one: a tag_ret cell reads "64.0, 100.0". The column looks fine in glimpse(), but that value is silently NA. Only problems() tells you.

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
text:
Challenge 1: Type Detective (15 min)
Question: why did WEIGHT break R’s guess in 22 rows?

Base: read WEIGHT as text, find the values that are not plain numbers, convert with parse_number(), prove it with glimpse() and an NA count
Extension: what does ".9 /K" become? Is that correct? What would you ask the data owner?

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
section: Cycle 2: The Rows And Columns You Need
text:
Cycle 2: The Rows And Columns You Need
stocking_core <- stocked |>
  select(year, month, day, lake, state_prov, site, agency,
         species, stage, no_stocked, length, weight)

nrow(stocking_core)

superior_lat <- stocking_core |>
  filter(lake == "SU", species == "LAT")     # comma = AND
nrow(superior_lat)

stocking_core |> filter(species %in% c("CHS", "COS"))  # one column, many values
stocking_core |> filter(between(year, 1990, 1999))
stocking_core |> filter(!is.na(month))
superior_lat  |> arrange(desc(no_stocked))

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
text:
Where Did The Rows Go?
stocking_core |> filter(length > 100)    |> nrow()
stocking_core |> filter(!(length > 100)) |> nrow()

These two do not add up to the total
filter() drops rows where the condition is NA
Missing values never pass a test, and never fail one

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
text:
Challenge 2: Three Manager Questions (15 min)
One pipeline each. Report nrow() each time.

Lake trout (LAT) stocked in Lake Superior (SU) by Wisconsin since 2000, largest first
Chinook or coho (CHS, COS) in Lake Michigan (MI) in the 1990s
Walleye (WAE) in Lake Erie (ER) with no recorded month

Extension: a question with 0 rows. Does 0 rows mean it never happened?

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
text: Break (10 min)

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
text:
Cycle 3: New Variables
stocking_core <- stocking_core |>          # reassign to keep it
  mutate(
    fish_thousands = round(no_stocked / 1000, 1),
    decade = (year %/% 10) * 10             # 1987 %/% 10 is 198
  ) |>
  relocate(decade, .after = year)

write_csv(stocking_core,
          here("class", "data", "processed", "stocking_core.csv"))
# never overwrite the raw file

title: Module 04: Clean and Shape Columns
text:
Integrated Challenge (15 min)
Lake Huron walleye, 2010s: after dropping events with no recorded length, which event stocked the largest fish? How many events did you drop?

Base: rows before, drop missing length, rows after, sort, answer in a comment
Extension: count(stage) shows 17 codes. How many real stages? Make them consistent (hint: str_to_lower())
Discuss: if a third of events have no length, is “largest fish” trustworthy?

Open class/first_report.qmd
YAML header: title, author, format

Break it on purpose, read the error, fix it

title: Module 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
Slide Accessibility Note

Title Background Image Alt-Text: A close-up image of a computer screen displaying multiple R error messages in red text, symbolizing the debugging process.
Speaker Notes: These slides explain the fundamental nature of R objects and how to diagnose errors.

title: Module 02: Objects & Debugging
Module 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
How To Use Today

Read the error message before touching the code.
Use the Environment pane as a diagnostic tool.
Fix the cause, not just the symptom.

Download the Module 02 follow-along script (.R)

Speaker Notes: This week is about developing a debugging habit. The slides should help students remember the flow: inspect, diagnose, fix, verify.

title: Module 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
R is for Objects

Everything that exists in R is an object.
Everything that happens is a function.
Objects have types (numeric, character, logical).


Speaker Notes: In R, everything you create—a single number, a list of names, or a giant dataset—is an ‘object’. We interact with these objects using ‘functions’. Today we learn how to see inside these objects and understand their ‘type’.

title: Module 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
Learning Objectives

Create and name R objects.
Identify common data types.
Inspect data frames in the Environment.
Interpret and fix common R errors.


Speaker Notes: Our goal is to move from being ‘scared’ of error messages to ‘reading’ them. By the end of today, you should be able to identify why a function fails based on the data type you give it.

title: Module 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
Live Coding: Section 1

Creating vectors and data frames.
Breaking R on purpose.
Interpreting error messages.


Speaker Notes: We’ll start by building vectors. Then, I’m going to ask you to try and ‘break’ your code. Intentionally causing errors is one of the best ways to learn how R thinks.

title: Module 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: The Debugging Clinic

Open debug_this.R in your Assignment 02 repository.
Fix 3 intentional errors and explain each cause in a code comment above the fix.
Inspect a small soil dataset before deciding what to fix.
Extension: Convert a column type and create a logical pH check.
Base goal: Get the script running from top to bottom.
Extension goal: Explain each fix in plain language.

To get the repository: sign in to Classroom 50 with your GitHub account, select NRES800, and create Assignment 02 - Debugging Clinic. Clone it in Positron the same way as Assignment 01.

Speaker Notes: In this challenge, you are playing the role of a ‘Code Doctor’. I’ve provided a script that is sick—it won’t run. Your job is to diagnose the 3 main bugs and get it back to healthy, runnable status.

title: Module 02: Objects & Debugging
text:
Verification

Does the script run without errors from top to bottom?
Can you identify the object-name, data-type, and plotting errors?
Did you save debug_this.R and your explanation comments?
Did you replace the README paragraph with 2-3 sentences of your own?
We upload together at the start of class. This is the last supported upload; Assignment 03 is pushed from home.
Due Tuesday, Sep 22, 11:59 PM. Feedback arrives as an Issue in your repository.


Speaker Notes: If they can explain the error in one sentence and show the fix in the script, they have met the goal for the day.


Speaker Notes: Verification check: Run your script from top to bottom. If it stops, read the first error and inspect the named object before changing code. Remind students that this is the last time the upload is walked through in class: Assignment 03 (import and inspect) is already open in Classroom 50, is done at home, and is due Sunday, Sep 27. Point them to the Issues tab for their Module 01 feedback.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
Module 03: The Whole Game
section: Today: Turn Your Graph into an Assignment
text:
Today: Turn Your Graph into an Assignment

Accept the NRES800 organization invitation in GitHub.
In Classroom 50, sign in with that GitHub account, select NRES800, and create your private Assignment 01 repository.
Clone it and open assignment.R.
Rebuild the graph you explored: body mass vs. flipper length, colored by species.
Make it readable, explain one pattern in script comments, run it, commit, and push.

Due: Tuesday, September 15, 2026, 11:59 PM Central Time.

Speaker Notes: Start with the graph students explored before the break. The point is not to start a different exercise; it is to turn that exploratory graph into a small, reproducible submission. Demonstrate the workflow in this order: open the Classroom 50 assignment, create the private repository, clone it, open assignment.R, move the familiar ggplot() mapping into the assignment, run the script, inspect the plot, commit, and push. Before opening Classroom 50, confirm that students accepted their NRES800 GitHub organization invitation; they must sign in to Classroom 50 with that same account and select NRES800. Do not promise an accept link on this slide: show the current Classroom 50 page or post the link once the assignment is registered.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
text:
Choose One Git Path

GitHub Desktop: use it if it opens; no terminal required.
Positron’s built-in Source Control: use its Git panel if Git is installed; no terminal or separate GitHub extension is needed.
Both paths end the same way: clone → fetch/pull → edit → commit → push → verify on GitHub.
If an app will not open, your repository is safe on GitHub: take a screenshot and use the other path or ask for help.


Speaker Notes: Students do not need the gh command-line tool for this assignment. Start by asking who has a working GitHub Desktop and direct them to that path. For students using Positron, demonstrate New Folder from Git and the Source Control icon in the left Activity Bar. Explain the vocabulary before clicking anything: clone makes the first local copy, fetch checks for remote changes without changing their files, pull brings those changes into the local copy, commit makes a named local checkpoint, and push sends that checkpoint to GitHub. The book’s “Getting your assignment repository” section gives the click-by-click directions for both paths.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
section: Brand-New Positron User? Use Built-In Source Control to Clone First.
text:
Brand-New Positron User? Use Built-In Source Control to Clone First.

On GitHub: Code → HTTPS → Copy.
In Positron’s built-in Source Control: choose New Folder from Git.
Paste the address, choose your class-work folder, and select Create Folder.
When Positron finishes, open the new folder; then open assignment.R.

Do not start with File → Open Folder. That comes after the clone creates your local repository.

Speaker Notes: This sequence is specifically for students who have never cloned a repository. They cannot open an assignment folder before one exists on their computer. Demonstrate the GitHub Code → HTTPS copy, then Positron’s built-in New Folder from Git command. It is the GUI route for clone, fetch, pull, commit, and push; students do not need a terminal or a separate GitHub extension. Only after cloning finishes should they use the Explorer to open assignment.R. For students who have already cloned the repository, File → Open Folder is appropriate for returning to that existing local folder.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
section: Why Keep GitHub in the Loop?
text:
Why Keep GitHub in the Loop?


Illustration by Allison Horst, CC BY 4.0.


Speaker Notes: This image is a visual metaphor, not a required decoding task. Say the point plainly: GitHub gives a project named checkpoints and a shared version of the work; without those, it is easy to lose track of which file is current. Connect the three visible ideas to today’s actions: clone the shared starting point, commit named checkpoints, and push the current version for others to review.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
text:
How To Use Today

Type along in the follow-along script.
Ask questions during the checkpoints.
Keep the goal small: one plot, one interpretation, one push.

Download the Assignment 01 follow-along script (.R)

Speaker Notes: This deck is the narrative layer, not the whole lesson. We will use it to orient ourselves, but the instructor script is the real teaching artifact.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
text:
Why the “Whole Game”?

We start by doing, not just installing.
You will load data, make a plot, and interpret it TODAY.
We will spend the rest of the semester unpacking HOW it works.


Speaker Notes: Welcome to NRES 800. We use a ‘Whole Game’ approach, inspired by David Perkins. Instead of spending weeks learning about file types and syntax, we are going to build a full analysis today. This gives you the ‘big picture’ context for everything else we’ll learn.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
text:
Learning Objectives

Create a private weekly repository through Classroom 50 and clone it.
Move a familiar ggplot2 graph into a reproducible R script.
Run the complete script and inspect the resulting plot.
Commit and push a reproducible result to GitHub.


Speaker Notes: These four objectives are the technical foundation of the course. If you can do these four things by the end of today, you are 100% on track.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
text:
Today’s Dataset: Palmer Penguins

Data on three penguin species in Antarctica.
Variables: bill length, flipper length, body mass, sex.
A classic dataset for learning visualization.


Speaker Notes: The palmerpenguins dataset is a modern alternative to the classic ‘iris’ dataset. It’s real ecological data collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman at the Palmer Station.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
text:
Live Coding: Section 1

Open your project in RStudio.
Open scripts/week_01_follow_along.R.
Type along as we build the plot.


Speaker Notes: Now, please switch over to RStudio. We are going to build our first plot. Remember: don’t just watch me—type the code yourself. The muscle memory of typing is how you learn the syntax.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
text:
The Challenge [45 mins]
Problem: The 30-Minute Analyst

Load the palmerpenguins data.
Create a scatterplot of body mass vs flipper length.
Color the points by species.
Extension: Add professional labels and a theme.
Base goal: Make the plot work and make the mapping correct.
Extension goal: Make the plot readable without explanation.


Speaker Notes: You have 45 minutes to work on this challenge. If you finish the base goal early, try the extension. The extension asks you to add labels like title, x-axis, and y-axis.

title: Module 03: The Whole Game
text:
Verification

We’re going to use a package called ‘here’ that builds paths relative to your project file, making your code portable and reproducible.

text:
The Data: Great Lakes Commercial Catch

Great Lakes Fishery Commission commercial fish production
65,706 rows x 7 columns, 1867-2015, six lakes
values = catch in thousands of pounds
Used exactly as released. Via TidyTuesday (2021-06-08)


Same agency as last week’s stocking data. Ask: what would a fisheries manager want summarized from this?

title: Module 05: Summaries and Decisions
text:
Vocabulary








Term
Meaning




summary
one number that stands for many rows: a count, total, mean


grouping
group_by() splits rows; summarize() returns one row per group


na.rm = TRUE
drop NA before computing: a decision to report, not a fix


total row
a row that already sums other rows; include it and you double count


denominator
what a percentage is “out of”; change it, change the answer

title: Module 05: Summaries and Decisions
Module 05: Summaries and Decisions
text:
Why Is The Sum NA?

21,916 of 65,706 values are NA (a third of the file)
One unknown value makes the total unknown; R refuses to guess
na.rm = TRUE drops them. That is your decision
So report n_missing right beside the total, every time


sum(is.na(values)): is.na() gives TRUE/FALSE, sum() counts the TRUEs.

text:
How case_when() Reads

Each line: if this ~ then that
Lines are checked top to bottom; the first TRUE wins
.default catches every row no line matched (forget it: NA)
Always count() the result to check it


era = case_when(
  year < 2000 ~ "1950-1999",   # first: now 1867 lands here too
  year < 1900 ~ "1867-1899",   # never reached
  ...
)
